judges.rationale: I recomputed cluster coverage using only verified-real findings (raw clusterCoverage counts false-positive touches, which don't count as surfaced real issues). M1 is the runaway winner: 14 real findings mapping to 14 distinct clusters — double the runner-up — including 5 issues no other model surfaced as real (X3 trusted-provenance rendering, P4 stale draft copy, P8 missing head-dedupe, P17 FAILED-run retry loop, P19 pre-dedupe get_pr). M7 is second with 8 real findings across 7 clusters (S2/W4 migration conflict, W6 receiver-linkage gap, W11 internal=True dead leg, plus unique S10 branch-fallback misbinding). M2 is third: 7 real across 6 clusters, with 3 uniques (Y4, Q12, Q19) and strong hits on the two biggest issues (Y5/Q5, Q18). M6, M4, and M5 all cover exactly 4 distinct real clusters; M6 ranks ahead because 2 of its 4 are unique to it (J4 canonical-reviewer contract contradiction, L9 fire-and-forget drop) and it landed 6 real findings, while M4 (U13, U14, V8, V9) and M5 (M9, M13, M14, K6) surfaced nothing exclusive; M4 edges M5 because its clusters were rarer catches (each found-real by only 2-3 models vs M5's mostly widely-found issues). Verified-real rates: M6 6/16 (37.5%), M7 8/24 (33.3%), M1 14/44 (31.8%), M2 7/36 (19.4%), M3 3/17 (17.6%), M5 4/28 (14.3%), M4 4/30 (13.3%). M6 wins cleanly: highest rate AND the densest signal per emission — 4 of its 6 reals are must_fix (J5, L3, L4, L6 — migration-leaf conflict and receiver-leg linkage gaps), so a reviewer reading M6's output wades through the least junk per real bug. M7 is close behind (S2, W4, W6 must_fix) with only 16 junk findings total. M1's rate is respectable and includes the dead-carve-out must_fix P12, but it bought its 14 reals with 30 junk emissions — the largest absolute wade-through burden on the panel — and its reals skew consider-grade (8/14), capping it at third. The bottom four all sit under 20%, and their junk includes outright fabrications, which is the worst kind: M2 misquoted a regex into a nonexistent \s typo (Y16) and asserted disproven Django on_commit semantics (Y13); M3's tiny 17-finding output still contained two claims false against the PR head (T1 tach.toml, R2 max_migration); M5 emitted stale-checkout hallucinations declaring the PR's own facades nonexistent (M8, K9) plus the false resolver-registration claim K7. M4 avoided fabrications but has the worst rate (13.3%), zero must_fix reals, and duplicated its own noise (U8/U9, V6/V7 in the same cluster), earning last place.

No model owns an exclusive must_fix — every must_fix falls into three heavy clusters: A dead carve-out leg (internal=True), B receiver-leg provenance spoofing (no PR-to-run linkage), C migration-0019 leaf conflict. M7 is #1 as the only model touching all three with verified findings (S2+W4 must_fix on C in both runs, W6 must_fix on B, W11 should_fix on A) plus the unique security-adjacent S10 (branch fallback authorizing an unrelated run as self-driving). M2 is #3: must_fix on A in both runs (Y5, Q5) and on B (Q18), plus should_fix Y8 (retry path blocking stale-approval dismissal), but it missed the CI-breaking C, and its unique catches (Y4, Q12, Q19) are low-impact copy/UX considers. M1 is #4: only one must_fix (P12 on A) and B only at should_fix (X20), but the strongest should_fix layer — 5 total including two exclusives, X3 (TRUSTED provenance block rendered with zero engine-side verification) and P8 (webhook-leg double-review of the same head) — and the widest cluster coverage (36/74). M3 is #5: it nailed the two heaviest runtime clusters as must_fix (T10 on A, T7 on B) but delivered only 3 real findings total and missed C. M5 is #6: K6 must_fix on C and M9 should_fix on B, but missed A and added only two shared considers. M4 is #7 by a wide margin: zero must_fix, all four real findings (U14, V8, U13, V9) are shared mid-tier clusters, and it missed A, B, and C entirely.
